title: A single-covariate benchmark against omitted composite structure
question: Does the bias from dropping the strongest measured covariate bound the residual bias from several omitted variables, and does a scaled benchmark calibrate?
design: Unanchored binary-outcome MAIC with four measured covariates and one, three or six correlated omitted covariates of varying strength; leave-one-covariate-out benchmark, unscaled and scaled by sqrt(q), by the oracle correlation-adjusted factor and by q; coverage of the true residual bias. 21 cells, 1000 replicates each.
answer: No. With three or six omitted variables each no stronger than the strongest measured covariate, the leave-one-covariate-out benchmark covered the true residual bias in at most 7% of analyses, the bias being 1.4 to 5.7 times the benchmark. Scaling by the square root of the number of omitted variables did not fix it; scaling by the number itself did when each omitted variable was weaker than the strongest measured one. The benchmark also shrank as omitted structure grew, through odds-ratio non-collapsibility.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: plain benchmark coverage 0.00 to 0.07 for q of 3 or 6 with each omitted variable at most as strong as the strongest measured.
Scaled by sqrt(q): coverage 0.00 to 0.76; by the oracle correlation-adjusted factor: 0.00 to 0.98; by q: 0.99 to 1.00 at half strength and 0.57 to 0.67 at equal strength.
Median benchmark fell from 0.163 (one weak omitted variable) to 0.067 (six strong correlated ones) while the true bias rose from 0.08 to 0.56 and beyond.
not_answered: Omitted variables shifted in the same direction; one overlap level; negative-control route not run. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: A's marginal log odds in the target (the unanchored comparison's A side) and MAIC's residual bias
methods_compared: benchmark times the oracle correlation-adjusted factor
